lesson.title: A New Deal for the American People: Roosevelt's Rise
lesson.summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt's landslide 1932 victory over a badly discredited Hoover brought an energetic, optimistic new leader to the White House who promised bold experimentation to fight the Depression.
lesson.body:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born in 1882 into a wealthy family in New York's Hudson Valley, a distant cousin of former president Theodore Roosevelt. Before his presidency, he served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy under Woodrow Wilson and ran as the Democratic candidate for vice president on the losing 1920 ticket. In 1921, he was struck by a paralytic illness, widely believed at the time and long afterward to be polio, which left him unable to walk unaided for the rest of his life. He worked hard, with considerable success, to limit how much the public saw of his disability.

Roosevelt was elected Governor of New York in 1928 and reelected in 1930, building a reputation during the early years of the Depression for pragmatic, active relief efforts, including the creation of a state relief agency to aid the unemployed. That record of hands-on action stood in sharp contrast to the more cautious, voluntarist approach Hoover was taking in Washington, a contrast covered in the earlier chapter on Hoover's response.

At the 1932 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Roosevelt accepted the party's presidential nomination with a speech promising, in a phrase that would give the entire era its name, "a new deal for the American people." Given the suffering visible in the Hoovervilles spreading across the country and the shock of the Bonus Army's violent eviction from Washington just months earlier, voters were ready for a change. Roosevelt defeated Hoover in a landslide that November, winning the large majority of the electoral vote.

Because the Twentieth Amendment had not yet shifted future inaugurations to January, Roosevelt was not sworn in until March 4, 1933, the last presidential inauguration held on that date. The long interval between the election and the inauguration proved painful, as the banking crisis described in an earlier chapter grew even worse during those months. In his inaugural address, Roosevelt sought to restore public confidence with the famous line that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." Within days, his administration would begin the burst of legislative activity known as the New Deal, the subject of the next chapter.
